title: Looking back: the daily banis
hook: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, heard in order

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurta Gaddi: in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh passed the guruship to the Granth, and your line, the eternal guru. Today we turn around and look back at the year.

Six banis. One day. A Sikh home before dawn: a kettle, a dark window, a voice already reading. By breakfast, several prayers have passed. At dusk, another. At bedtime, one more, with the lights low. This year you met each of those prayers on its own, block by block, sometimes for weeks. Today you hear them as they're lived: in order, one day long. Looking back: the daily banis.
screen: `SIX BANIS, ONE DAY.` → `MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.` → `HEARD IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Start in the dark. Amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, is when the Sikh code of conduct asks a Sikh to rise, bathe and begin. After the Japji comes the Jaap Sahib, which Sikhs know as Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise, all short lines and quick meters. You met its line in the spring: namastvam akaale, salutation to the One beyond time. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, ten verses under the heading by Your grace: the poet has seen monks, yogis and mighty kings by the thousand, and says all of it is worth nothing without love. Then, in some homes, the Benti Chaupai, a prayer for shelter: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, give me Your hand and keep me safe. Then Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib, the song of bliss, which opens with a cry of joy: anand bhaiaa meree maae, I am in bliss, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. That's the morning. Then the day itself: work, traffic, dishes, people. The banis don't ask anyone to leave it. They frame it. At dusk, as work ends, Rehras, the evening prayer. It opens with So Dar, the door where the Creator sits and cares for all. And last, at bedtime, Kirtan Sohila, five short hymns, beginning jai ghar keerat aakheeai: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung. The same hymns are sung at funerals, so the close of a day and the close of a life share one song. Notice what the order does. Praise first, before anything has happened. Shelter for the hours ahead. Joy. A door at dusk. A song for sleep. The whole day, held between words.
screen: `AMRITVELA: JAAP AND THE SAVAIYE.` · `SHELTER AND BLISS: CHAUPAI, ANAND.` · `DUSK: REHRAS, AS WORK ENDS.` · `NIGHT: SOHILA, THE SONG FOR SLEEP.` · then, large: `THE DAY, HELD.`

segments.voice: Say one line from each, slowly, aloud or under your breath, with a full breath between: namastvam akaale; tav prasad, by Your grace; hamree karo hath dai rachhaa; anand bhaiaa meree maae; so dar; jai ghar keerat aakheeai. If a line won't come, say it in English, and let that be enough. Then rest in the quiet after the sixth.
Looking back. Turning around near the top of the year to see the daily banis together: Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras and Sohila, from before dawn to bedtime.
Your line: the day, held. Words at both edges, and the day between. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs say the Japji, Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Savaiye in the early morning, often with Chaupai and Anand Sahib, then Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila before sleep.

fork.setup: the work is done and the light is going. which bani do many Sikhs say now?
fork.reveal: Rehras is the dusk prayer; Jaap belongs to the morning, and Asa di Var is sung before sunrise.

original.note: Punjabi: the word of the Gurus, the hymns themselves; the daily banis are the ones said each day.

trapdoor: what you thought: the daily prayers are a checklist to get through.
what it means: they frame a whole day, praise at dawn, shelter, joy, a prayer at dusk, a song for sleep.
what a scholar hears: the set mixes hymns of Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan with compositions Sikhs attribute to the Tenth Guru, and Kirtan Sohila doubles as the funeral hymn.
guess: seeing the year's daily banis side by side
reading the Granth from its last page first
regretting the mistakes of the past year

chat.says: Your Sikh friend prays at dawn, at dusk and at bedtime. Is it the same prayer each time?
options: No: Jaap and more at dawn, Rehras as work ends, Kirtan Sohila before sleep.
Yes, the Japji is said three times, since it's the only prayer that's set.
The dawn prayers are for monks; everyone else says only the bedtime one.
chat.meaning: The daily banis frame the day: Japji, Jaap and the Savaiye before dawn, Rehras at dusk as work ends, and Kirtan Sohila at bedtime.

notes: Fresh review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens with 'Picture'; cut the folk etymology of Rehras as 'provisions for the road' (teach, screen head, myth, trapdoor), which no cited source gives; amritvela rising now attributed to the Rehat Maryada rather than 'many Sikhs'; Jaap attributed as 'Sikhs know as Guru Gobind Singh's'; 'in many homes' softened to 'some'.

The Sikh Rehat Maryada lists Japji, Jaap and the ten Savaiye for the morning; Chaupai and Anand are said in the morning 'in many homes' (and by many Amritdhari Sikhs as the five banis). Confirm wording.
Transliterated lines (namastvam akaale, hamree karo hath dai rachhaa, anand bhaiaa meree maae, so dar, jai ghar keerat aakheeai) follow the y2 outline; Keeper to confirm transliteration.

Jaap, Savaiye and Chaupai are attributed to Guru Gobind Singh by the Rehat Maryada and Sikh tradition; some academic scholars debate parts of Dasam Granth authorship. The trapdoor now says 'compositions Sikhs attribute to the Tenth Guru' (and adds Guru Ram Das, whose hymns are in Rehras and Sohila); Keeper to confirm whether the teach should keep the plain attribution.
Savaiye paraphrase combines verse 1 (monks, siddhas, yogis) and verse 2 (mighty kings); confirm.
